pullQuote: I’d choose A2UI for a shared interface contract that constrains agent capabilities while letting people interact through web and native components.
testimonial: I would choose A2UI as the interface foundation, rather than force every platform into one rendering framework. Its Basic Catalog, incremental updateComponents messages, and typed callRendererFunction mechanism connect agent-generated interfaces, application state, and explicitly exposed operations. Compared with Tamagui, I accept more catalog integration and platform-version coordination instead of a ready-made shared React component layer. I would still enforce authorization in application services and test accessibility on each renderer; a schema is not a substitute for either.
evaluations:
**Fluent UI** — Fluent offers a credible cross-platform design language, but not one cross-platform implementation: the supplied repository contains React and Web Components, while [Apple](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-apple) and [Android](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-android) have separate native libraries. The [React suite](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui/blob/master/packages/react-components/react-components/README.md) uses FluentProvider and themes, making it attractive for Microsoft-aligned products. I would have to coordinate component behavior across those implementations and add a shared agent action contract. That is workable, but A2UI supplies more of the cross-renderer agent interface I am choosing for.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — I particularly value the separation between React Stately state, React Aria behavior, and Spectrum presentation; the [repository](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum) explicitly distinguishes reusable state from web component implementations. Its [quality documentation](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/react-aria/accessibility.html) describes keyboard and focus handling, testing with named screen readers, and localization across more than 30 languages. This would be my strongest web accessibility foundation, but cross-platform state reuse does not mean native React Aria widgets ship with it. Native renderers and a permissioned action interface would address that gap; I would happily use Aria-backed components inside an A2UI web catalog.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — The [library](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui) provides React components built on Radix, Tailwind 4 tokens, and ChatGPT-oriented styling, not the agent transport or application authorization layer. OpenAI’s [integration guide](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/chatgpt-ui.md) now recommends MCP Apps for the bridge and treats this component library as optional. I would choose it for a polished ChatGPT plugin, but an iframe inside a native host is not native widget rendering. Broader platform implementations would be needed for it to become my common interface foundation.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its [shared action architecture](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview) is an excellent answer to agents operating applications: defineAction powers React hooks, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI instead of maintaining separate business logic. The [authorization documentation](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/actions-access-control/) adds resource policies, authorize guards, and needsApproval, although these restrictions require deliberate configuration. My trade-off is adopting a substantial application architecture around shared SQL state and a server runtime, rather than a renderer-neutral interface contract. I did not establish equivalent first-party native widget coverage from the sources reviewed; documented native integrations would make it a stronger overall contender.

**Radix UI** — Radix is a focused, unstyled web interaction foundation, with useful control over markup through [asChild composition](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition). That flexibility has concrete obligations: custom children must spread props, accept refs, and preserve accessible element semantics. I would use it beneath a branded web catalog, but it does not itself solve native rendering or expose application operations to agents. Adding a validated component catalog and a shared action service would address those needs without asking Radix to become an agent framework.

**MCP Apps** — The [specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx) standardizes ui:// resources, tool linkage, JSON-RPC communication, mandatory iframe sandboxing, and declared CSP requirements. This is a strong distribution and isolation layer for interactive tools across compatible assistant hosts, with [host support explicitly varying](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps). Its current HTML resource model does not provide native component rendering or a design system. I would use MCP Apps as a delivery channel, potentially around an A2UI renderer, rather than make it the entire interface foundation.

**AI Elements** — Conversation, message, reasoning, and tool displays make this a useful presentation layer, but they are copied React components rather than an agent execution or native-rendering architecture. Importantly, the [captured repository](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) announces deprecation at the end of November 2026, while the [shadcn migration documentation](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements) already describes replacement patterns and elements without replacements. Existing copies keep working; deprecation does not invalidate shipped applications. For a new project I would use the successor patterns and supply a separate runtime and native implementation, rather than adopt the outgoing repository.

**shadcn/ui** — Its [open-code distribution model](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs) gives teams ownership of component source, while the [MCP server](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp) lets coding agents discover and install registry items. Those are development-time advantages, not automatic runtime access to the finished application. Current AI Elements patterns also provide useful approval and tool-progress interfaces. I would accept ownership of upstream reconciliation for a web product, but for this brief I still need native implementations and a constrained runtime contract; using shadcn components behind A2UI catalogs preserves its strengths.

**MUI** — MUI offers a substantial React web component system with [ThemeProvider, createTheme, and CSS theme variables](https://mui.com/material-ui/customization/theming/); its [default installation](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/installation/) uses Emotion and React DOM. I would favor it for a conventional, component-rich business application where theming and established controls dominate the decision. It is not the same implementation as Android’s Material 3, so choosing the Material visual language does not eliminate native work. A shared token pipeline and agent-callable service layer would make it fit, but those are additional architecture rather than capabilities supplied by MUI itself.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — [MaterialTheme, dynamic color, and Material 3 Expressive](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) provide a strong Android-native presentation system. Compose’s [semantics tree](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics) exposes roles, state, actions, and custom accessibility actions to assistive services and tests, which is much more useful than pixels alone. I would use it for the Android host, but the supplied Android toolkit is not by itself a web-and-Apple implementation. A2UI’s [SDK matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) documents a Compose adapter at v0.9.1, so a shared contract is possible, with explicit version negotiation rather than assumed v1.0 parity.

**Tamagui** — Tamagui is my strongest alternative for a shared, developer-authored React web/native component layer: its [compiler](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction) extracts atomic CSS and flattens components, with runtime fallback when optimization is unavailable. The [Adapt primitive](https://tamagui.dev/ui/adapt) can move a Select or Popover into a Sheet while retaining content and open state, addressing real platform interaction differences. I prefer A2UI here because I want the agent contract to work beyond React and React Native. Tamagui would require a separately defined, validated catalog and permissioned operations layer; that is an integration cost, not a weakness in its styling architecture.

**A2UI** — I would choose its separation of Core SDK, Agent SDK, framework adapter, and component catalog: the [SDK documentation](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) describes incremental state updates, schema validation, native accessibility mappings, and web, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Compose renderers. The [RPC implementation](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/typescript/core/web_core/src/rpc/rpc-handler.ts) checks caller permissions and validates arguments before executing registered functions, giving me a concrete boundary rather than arbitrary generated code. It is not a complete branded design system, and parity needs attention: Compose is listed at v0.9.1, while the [SwiftUI adapter](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/swift/swiftui/README.md) documents group-hint, live-region, and older-OS subtree-reset limitations. I would address these with negotiated feature subsets, carefully implemented catalogs, platform accessibility tests, and service-side authorization; I reviewed the implementation and tests, but did not execute them.

**json-render** — This is a close contender: [defineCatalog, defineRegistry, and SpecStream](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/core/README.md) constrain generated interfaces to application-defined components and progressively apply JSON patches. Its [React Native renderer](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md) is real, with standard mobile components, two-way bindings, action providers, and an external StateStore—not merely a future native claim. I would likely prefer it for a TypeScript team targeting web and React Native. For this broader brief, A2UI’s documented SwiftUI and Compose paths are more compelling; json-render would need corresponding adapters, and either choice still needs authorization and accessibility validation beyond schema correctness.

**CopilotKit** — [AG-UI events, shared state, frontend tools, and human-in-the-loop flows](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit) make this a strong application-agent integration layer rather than just a chat widget. The [React Native quickstart](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/react-native) documents a headless entry point and native chat components, but explicitly marks generative UI experimental and requires careful Metro/polyfill setup. I would choose it when agent orchestration and collaborative workflows are the primary problem. For my selection, it is a useful companion to A2UI rather than the common rendering contract itself; I would first verify the needed native generative-UI features and dependency setup on release builds.

**Base UI** — Its [compound React components and portal architecture](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start) give precise control without prescribing a visual theme. The [accessibility guide](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/accessibility) distinguishes implemented keyboard/focus behavior from application responsibilities such as visible focus, contrast, and labels—an important distinction for agent-generated compositions. I would use it as a web catalog foundation, not as the complete cross-platform solution. Styled recipes, native equivalents, and an agent action contract would address the missing layers; the objection is scope, not lack of useful accessibility engineering.

**Vercel UI SDK** — This is more than coding-agent documentation: its [agent bridge](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent) exposes snapshot, query, and act over component state and APIs, while a framework-free behavior core supports five web adapters. Its [permission model](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/permissions) includes allow callbacks, confirmation markers, redaction, and cancellable changes, but actions are accepted by default and multi-step calls are not transactional. That direct runtime operability makes it especially interesting for shared human/agent web interfaces. I would want stable APIs, explicit permission policies, and native adapters before choosing it over A2UI; the [repository](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui) still labels it beta.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui) provides declarative views, model-to-view data flow, adaptive controls, and Apple-framework integration; the [HIG accessibility guidance](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) adds concrete requirements for Dynamic Type, contrast, and auditing. I would pair it with the separate [App Intents framework](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents) to expose structured actions and entities to Apple Intelligence, Siri, and Shortcuts. This is a compelling Apple-native stack, but it does not supply web or Android rendering. I would keep SwiftUI as an A2UI host implementation and share domain operations across platforms, rather than make Apple’s ecosystem the universal contract.

**Ouro UI** — Ouro’s distinction between human-facing HX and agent-facing AX is unusually concrete: the [AX kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax.md) derives CLI/MCP interfaces from command declarations and supplies typed outcomes, dry runs, receipts, and external conformance checks. The [web library](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui) uses copy-in React/Base UI components, while [Ouro UI for Apple](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple) adds SwiftUI components, App Intents support, and shared token provenance. I would not dismiss it as web-only, but Apple remains pre-1.0 with a substantially smaller component set, and the [published platform matrix](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core) covers web and Apple rather than Android. Broader native coverage and demonstrated parity would address my main objection; its explicit action outcomes are a pattern I would borrow regardless.

**Flutter** — Flutter offers a genuine single-codebase web, mobile, and desktop toolkit with Material/Cupertino widgets and its own rendering architecture, as the [repository](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) documents. Its [web accessibility layer](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility) translates Semantics into HTML, but is opt-in by default; I would explicitly enable it and test browser-agent interaction rather than assume canvas rendering is either inaccessible or automatically equivalent to DOM controls. The [GenUI SDK](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui) adds catalog-driven agent interaction, although it is documented as alpha. Flutter is attractive for a unified Dart application, but A2UI lets me retain different host frameworks instead of requiring that commitment.

**Chakra UI** — Chakra’s [createSystem, semantic tokens, recipes, and slot recipes](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview) provide a cohesive and configurable React web design system, including strict token typing when generated types stay synchronized. Its [MCP server](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server) exposes component documentation, examples, tokens, and migration assistance to coding agents; it does not by itself grant runtime control of an application. I would choose it for fast development of a themed web interface, but native rendering and a shared agent capability contract remain additional work. A constrained catalog using Chakra on web and corresponding native components would address those requirements.

actions.pullQuote: I’d choose A2UI for a shared interface contract that constrains agent capabilities while letting people interact through web and native components.
actions.testimonial: I would choose A2UI as the interface foundation, rather than force every platform into one rendering framework. Its Basic Catalog, incremental updateComponents messages, and typed callRendererFunction mechanism connect agent-generated interfaces, application state, and explicitly exposed operations. Compared with Tamagui, I accept more catalog integration and platform-version coordination instead of a ready-made shared React component layer. I would still enforce authorization in application services and test accessibility on each renderer; a schema is not a substitute for either.
actions.evaluations:
**Fluent UI** — Fluent offers a credible cross-platform design language, but not one cross-platform implementation: the supplied repository contains React and Web Components, while [Apple](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-apple) and [Android](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-android) have separate native libraries. The [React suite](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui/blob/master/packages/react-components/react-components/README.md) uses FluentProvider and themes, making it attractive for Microsoft-aligned products. I would have to coordinate component behavior across those implementations and add a shared agent action contract. That is workable, but A2UI supplies more of the cross-renderer agent interface I am choosing for.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — I particularly value the separation between React Stately state, React Aria behavior, and Spectrum presentation; the [repository](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum) explicitly distinguishes reusable state from web component implementations. Its [quality documentation](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/react-aria/accessibility.html) describes keyboard and focus handling, testing with named screen readers, and localization across more than 30 languages. This would be my strongest web accessibility foundation, but cross-platform state reuse does not mean native React Aria widgets ship with it. Native renderers and a permissioned action interface would address that gap; I would happily use Aria-backed components inside an A2UI web catalog.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — The [library](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui) provides React components built on Radix, Tailwind 4 tokens, and ChatGPT-oriented styling, not the agent transport or application authorization layer. OpenAI’s [integration guide](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/chatgpt-ui.md) now recommends MCP Apps for the bridge and treats this component library as optional. I would choose it for a polished ChatGPT plugin, but an iframe inside a native host is not native widget rendering. Broader platform implementations would be needed for it to become my common interface foundation.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its [shared action architecture](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview) is an excellent answer to agents operating applications: defineAction powers React hooks, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI instead of maintaining separate business logic. The [authorization documentation](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/actions-access-control/) adds resource policies, authorize guards, and needsApproval, although these restrictions require deliberate configuration. My trade-off is adopting a substantial application architecture around shared SQL state and a server runtime, rather than a renderer-neutral interface contract. I did not establish equivalent first-party native widget coverage from the sources reviewed; documented native integrations would make it a stronger overall contender.

**Radix UI** — Radix is a focused, unstyled web interaction foundation, with useful control over markup through [asChild composition](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition). That flexibility has concrete obligations: custom children must spread props, accept refs, and preserve accessible element semantics. I would use it beneath a branded web catalog, but it does not itself solve native rendering or expose application operations to agents. Adding a validated component catalog and a shared action service would address those needs without asking Radix to become an agent framework.

**MCP Apps** — The [specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx) standardizes ui:// resources, tool linkage, JSON-RPC communication, mandatory iframe sandboxing, and declared CSP requirements. This is a strong distribution and isolation layer for interactive tools across compatible assistant hosts, with [host support explicitly varying](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps). Its current HTML resource model does not provide native component rendering or a design system. I would use MCP Apps as a delivery channel, potentially around an A2UI renderer, rather than make it the entire interface foundation.

**AI Elements** — Conversation, message, reasoning, and tool displays make this a useful presentation layer, but they are copied React components rather than an agent execution or native-rendering architecture. Importantly, the [captured repository](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) announces deprecation at the end of November 2026, while the [shadcn migration documentation](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements) already describes replacement patterns and elements without replacements. Existing copies keep working; deprecation does not invalidate shipped applications. For a new project I would use the successor patterns and supply a separate runtime and native implementation, rather than adopt the outgoing repository.

**shadcn/ui** — Its [open-code distribution model](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs) gives teams ownership of component source, while the [MCP server](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp) lets coding agents discover and install registry items. Those are development-time advantages, not automatic runtime access to the finished application. Current AI Elements patterns also provide useful approval and tool-progress interfaces. I would accept ownership of upstream reconciliation for a web product, but for this brief I still need native implementations and a constrained runtime contract; using shadcn components behind A2UI catalogs preserves its strengths.

**MUI** — MUI offers a substantial React web component system with [ThemeProvider, createTheme, and CSS theme variables](https://mui.com/material-ui/customization/theming/); its [default installation](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/installation/) uses Emotion and React DOM. I would favor it for a conventional, component-rich business application where theming and established controls dominate the decision. It is not the same implementation as Android’s Material 3, so choosing the Material visual language does not eliminate native work. A shared token pipeline and agent-callable service layer would make it fit, but those are additional architecture rather than capabilities supplied by MUI itself.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — [MaterialTheme, dynamic color, and Material 3 Expressive](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) provide a strong Android-native presentation system. Compose’s [semantics tree](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics) exposes roles, state, actions, and custom accessibility actions to assistive services and tests, which is much more useful than pixels alone. I would use it for the Android host, but the supplied Android toolkit is not by itself a web-and-Apple implementation. A2UI’s [SDK matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) documents a Compose adapter at v0.9.1, so a shared contract is possible, with explicit version negotiation rather than assumed v1.0 parity.

**Tamagui** — Tamagui is my strongest alternative for a shared, developer-authored React web/native component layer: its [compiler](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction) extracts atomic CSS and flattens components, with runtime fallback when optimization is unavailable. The [Adapt primitive](https://tamagui.dev/ui/adapt) can move a Select or Popover into a Sheet while retaining content and open state, addressing real platform interaction differences. I prefer A2UI here because I want the agent contract to work beyond React and React Native. Tamagui would require a separately defined, validated catalog and permissioned operations layer; that is an integration cost, not a weakness in its styling architecture.

**A2UI** — I would choose its separation of Core SDK, Agent SDK, framework adapter, and component catalog: the [SDK documentation](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) describes incremental state updates, schema validation, native accessibility mappings, and web, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Compose renderers. The [RPC implementation](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/typescript/core/web_core/src/rpc/rpc-handler.ts) checks caller permissions and validates arguments before executing registered functions, giving me a concrete boundary rather than arbitrary generated code. It is not a complete branded design system, and parity needs attention: Compose is listed at v0.9.1, while the [SwiftUI adapter](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/swift/swiftui/README.md) documents group-hint, live-region, and older-OS subtree-reset limitations. I would address these with negotiated feature subsets, carefully implemented catalogs, platform accessibility tests, and service-side authorization; I reviewed the implementation and tests, but did not execute them.

**json-render** — This is a close contender: [defineCatalog, defineRegistry, and SpecStream](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/core/README.md) constrain generated interfaces to application-defined components and progressively apply JSON patches. Its [React Native renderer](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md) is real, with standard mobile components, two-way bindings, action providers, and an external StateStore—not merely a future native claim. I would likely prefer it for a TypeScript team targeting web and React Native. For this broader brief, A2UI’s documented SwiftUI and Compose paths are more compelling; json-render would need corresponding adapters, and either choice still needs authorization and accessibility validation beyond schema correctness.

**CopilotKit** — [AG-UI events, shared state, frontend tools, and human-in-the-loop flows](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit) make this a strong application-agent integration layer rather than just a chat widget. The [React Native quickstart](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/react-native) documents a headless entry point and native chat components, but explicitly marks generative UI experimental and requires careful Metro/polyfill setup. I would choose it when agent orchestration and collaborative workflows are the primary problem. For my selection, it is a useful companion to A2UI rather than the common rendering contract itself; I would first verify the needed native generative-UI features and dependency setup on release builds.

**Base UI** — Its [compound React components and portal architecture](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start) give precise control without prescribing a visual theme. The [accessibility guide](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/accessibility) distinguishes implemented keyboard/focus behavior from application responsibilities such as visible focus, contrast, and labels—an important distinction for agent-generated compositions. I would use it as a web catalog foundation, not as the complete cross-platform solution. Styled recipes, native equivalents, and an agent action contract would address the missing layers; the objection is scope, not lack of useful accessibility engineering.

**Vercel UI SDK** — This is more than coding-agent documentation: its [agent bridge](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent) exposes snapshot, query, and act over component state and APIs, while a framework-free behavior core supports five web adapters. Its [permission model](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/permissions) includes allow callbacks, confirmation markers, redaction, and cancellable changes, but actions are accepted by default and multi-step calls are not transactional. That direct runtime operability makes it especially interesting for shared human/agent web interfaces. I would want stable APIs, explicit permission policies, and native adapters before choosing it over A2UI; the [repository](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui) still labels it beta.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui) provides declarative views, model-to-view data flow, adaptive controls, and Apple-framework integration; the [HIG accessibility guidance](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) adds concrete requirements for Dynamic Type, contrast, and auditing. I would pair it with the separate [App Intents framework](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents) to expose structured actions and entities to Apple Intelligence, Siri, and Shortcuts. This is a compelling Apple-native stack, but it does not supply web or Android rendering. I would keep SwiftUI as an A2UI host implementation and share domain operations across platforms, rather than make Apple’s ecosystem the universal contract.

**Ouro UI** — Ouro’s distinction between human-facing HX and agent-facing AX is unusually concrete: the [AX kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax.md) derives CLI/MCP interfaces from command declarations and supplies typed outcomes, dry runs, receipts, and external conformance checks. The [web library](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui) uses copy-in React/Base UI components, while [Ouro UI for Apple](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple) adds SwiftUI components, App Intents support, and shared token provenance. I would not dismiss it as web-only, but Apple remains pre-1.0 with a substantially smaller component set, and the [published platform matrix](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core) covers web and Apple rather than Android. Broader native coverage and demonstrated parity would address my main objection; its explicit action outcomes are a pattern I would borrow regardless.

**Flutter** — Flutter offers a genuine single-codebase web, mobile, and desktop toolkit with Material/Cupertino widgets and its own rendering architecture, as the [repository](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) documents. Its [web accessibility layer](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility) translates Semantics into HTML, but is opt-in by default; I would explicitly enable it and test browser-agent interaction rather than assume canvas rendering is either inaccessible or automatically equivalent to DOM controls. The [GenUI SDK](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui) adds catalog-driven agent interaction, although it is documented as alpha. Flutter is attractive for a unified Dart application, but A2UI lets me retain different host frameworks instead of requiring that commitment.

**Chakra UI** — Chakra’s [createSystem, semantic tokens, recipes, and slot recipes](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview) provide a cohesive and configurable React web design system, including strict token typing when generated types stay synchronized. Its [MCP server](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server) exposes component documentation, examples, tokens, and migration assistance to coding agents; it does not by itself grant runtime control of an application. I would choose it for fast development of a themed web interface, but native rendering and a shared agent capability contract remain additional work. A constrained catalog using Chakra on web and corresponding native components would address those requirements.
